title: Walgreen Co. v. Sara Creek Property Co.
summary: An injunction enforcing a shopping-center pharmacy exclusivity clause was justified because projecting ten years of competitive losses would be costly and uncertain.

sections.Parties: Walgreen operated a pharmacy in Southgate Mall. Sara Creek was its landlord and had promised not to lease mall space to another store operating a pharmacy.
sections.Material Facts:
Sara Creek feared losing its anchor tenant and proposed to buy out that tenant and install Phar-Mor, a deep-discount store with a pharmacy. Its entrance would be within a few hundred feet of Walgreen’s. About ten years remained on Walgreen’s lease.

Sara Creek’s experts maintained that Walgreen’s competitive losses could be estimated. Walgreen’s witnesses stressed uncertainty about future sales, costs, and goodwill. The dispute concerned how to enforce the exclusivity promise, rather than whether a competing pharmacy might generate more total commercial value.
sections.Procedural History: After a hearing, the district court entered a permanent injunction preventing the competing pharmacy lease during Walgreen’s term. The Seventh Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: Were money damages adequate, or should a court enforce the exclusivity promise by injunction despite the possibility of a more valuable use of the premises?
sections.Holding: The injunction was appropriate on this record.
sections.Reasoning:
Posner compared the costs and benefits of the remedial alternatives. Damages would require estimating Walgreen’s revenues and costs over a decade, estimating the effect of the rival pharmacy, and discounting the losses. The underlying projections would be expensive and imprecise.

An injunction can allow the parties to negotiate the value of releasing the right. If Sara Creek’s gain exceeds Walgreen’s loss, a mutually beneficial payment may be possible. That is not a claim that negotiation is costless: the opinion recognizes supervision burdens, effects on third parties, and the possibility of expensive or failed bargaining when only these two parties can buy and sell the release.

The balance favored the injunction here, with damages remaining the default where the competing considerations are equal. The opinion’s numerical bargaining illustration is hypothetical; it is not a finding of the parties’ actual losses and gains.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Walgreen explains the adequacy inquiry through the practical costs of measuring loss, enforcing an order, and negotiating a release. Economic reasoning can support specific relief as well as damages.

topics.specific-performance: The court weighs the adequacy of damages and administration of an injunction; this is judicial remedial judgment.
topics.remedies: Choice of remedy depends on the comparative burdens and accuracy of available enforcement methods.
topics.efficient-breach: The opinion considers beneficial reallocation while recognizing that injunctions can permit negotiated release.

mnemonic.rationale: A pharmacy’s exclusive in the mall
